Just now

--

I started logging timestamps out of boredom. Then I noticed the fast ones and the slow ones were never for the same kind of job.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

A rejection landed in my inbox three minutes and forty seconds after I hit submit. I know the exact number because I’d started timing them, half as a joke, half because something about the speed felt off.
That one was for a data analyst role at a mid-size logistics company. I’d spent maybe twenty minutes tailoring the resume, another ten writing a cover letter that mentioned their actual product by name. Three minutes and forty seconds later, a form email told me they’d “carefully reviewed my application” and decided to move forward with other candidates. Nobody reviewed anything in three minutes and forty seconds. A machine read a resume, matched some keywords against a rubric, and closed the file before I’d even gotten back to my other tabs.
I’ve spent years working with SQL, building ETL pipelines, and wiring up REST API integrations in fintech, the kind of job where you get very used to the idea that a process either has a human in the loop or it doesn’t, and you can usually tell which just by watching how fast it moves. So when the rejections started coming back at machine speed, I started keeping a spreadsheet.
Why I started logging timestamps in the first place
The spreadsheet wasn’t supposed to be a project. I applied to a role on a Tuesday morning, got rejected by lunch, and thought, huh, that’s fast. So the next application, I wrote down the exact minute I submitted it. Then I did it for the one after that. Within two weeks I had thirty-one data points: submission timestamp, rejection timestamp (if any), company size as best I could tell from LinkedIn, and whether the job posting had been up for less than a week or more than a month.
I wasn’t trying to prove anything. I just wanted to know if my gut feeling, that some of these rejections felt instant and others felt considered, actually held up.
It held up more than I expected.
Of the thirty-one applications, nineteen came back with a rejection inside one business day. Of those nineteen, eleven arrived in under ten minutes. The fastest was one minute and change, for a support engineering role where I’d customized every line of the resume to match their stack. A human did not read that resume in sixty seconds. Something scored it, and the score didn’t clear the bar.
What the numbers actually showed
I split the thirty-one into two buckets: fast rejections (under one hour) and slow rejections or no response (over one hour, including the ones that just went quiet). Nineteen fast, twelve slow-or-silent.
Then I looked at what those two groups had in common, and it wasn’t what I expected. I’d assumed the fast rejections would cluster around jobs where I was a weak fit, and the slow ones around jobs where I was strong. That wasn’t really it. The real pattern was company size and how the posting was structured. Every single fast rejection came from a company with what looked like a centralized applicant tracking system, the kind with a long structured form asking for exact years of experience in six different skills before you could even upload a resume. Every one of the twelve slow-or-silent responses came from smaller companies or ones where the application was just an email address and a “tell us about yourself.”
That’s not a controversial finding if you think about it for five seconds. Big companies run high application volume through automated screening because they have to. But sitting inside my own data, watching my own job search get sorted by a machine in real time, felt different than reading a headline about it. The Q1 2026 job search numbers going around back this up too: something like two out of three job seekers this year report at least one AI rejection somewhere in their search, and I’d bet the real number is higher, because most of us never find out which side of the desk actually made the call.
The four-minute rejections versus the four-week ones
Here’s the part that actually changed how I apply. The four-minute rejections weren’t random. When I went back and looked at the job descriptions for those eleven ultra-fast no’s, ten of the eleven used a specific phrase or requirement I hadn’t matched closely enough. Not skill gaps, exactly, more like phrasing gaps. One posting wanted “data pipeline development,” and my resume said “ETL pipeline design.” Same job, different words, and the screener apparently cared about the words.
I started rewriting my resume, not to inflate anything, but to mirror the exact terminology in each posting before I submitted. Nothing dishonest, just translation. “REST API integration” became “API integration and third-party system connectivity” if that’s the phrase the posting used. “SQL reporting” became “SQL-based reporting and dashboarding” when that language showed up.
Nine applications after I started doing this, only three came back fast. The other six either went to a slower human-reviewed stage, or I got an actual response from a person, sometimes just a “thanks, moving on,” but a response from someone who’d clearly opened the file. That’s a small sample, and I’m not going to pretend nine data points prove a system. But it’s the difference between guessing and testing, and I’d rather test.
What “AI rejected me” actually means, technically
I want to be careful here because “AI rejected me” gets thrown around like it means one specific thing, and it doesn’t. Some of what’s screening resumes right now is genuinely a language model reading text and scoring fit. A lot of it is much dumber than that: keyword matching against a required-skills list, sometimes with weights, sometimes just pass or fail. The three-minute rejection I opened with was almost certainly the dumb version, not a model reasoning about my career, just a filter checking boxes.
That distinction matters because it changes what you can actually do about it. You can’t argue with a filter or appeal to its judgment. You can only feed it what it’s looking for, which is uncomfortable if you spent years being told that showing your real experience honestly is what gets you hired. Sometimes it is. Sometimes the filter just wants specific words in specific places, and the job of getting past it has nothing to do with whether you can do the work.
I don’t love that. I don’t think anyone applying to jobs right now loves that. But pretending it isn’t happening, and applying with the same resume language you’d use talking to a hiring manager over coffee, means you’re optimizing for a system that no longer exists at most companies over a certain size.
The offer that almost wasn’t
One of the slow-or-silent twelve turned into an actual conversation, then a phone screen, then an offer, three weeks after I’d basically written it off. I’d applied on a Sunday night, heard nothing for eleven days, and had mentally filed it under “gone.” Then a recruiter emailed apologizing for the delay, said they’d had a hiring freeze scare internally that got resolved, and asked if I was still interested.
I bring this up because the spreadsheet made me impatient in a way that wasn’t always useful. Fast rejections trained me to expect fast everything, and slow silence started to feel like automatic bad news. It wasn’t. Some of the best conversations in this search came from postings that took two or three weeks to respond to at all, because a human being was actually reading things in between other parts of their job.
The lesson isn’t “be patient,” exactly. It’s that speed tells you about the process, not about your chances. A three-minute no tells you a filter didn’t like your keywords. A three-week silence tells you almost nothing at all.
What I do differently now
I still keep the spreadsheet. I check the posting for exact phrasing before I write a word of the resume, and I stopped assuming any single rejection means anything about my actual skills, because increasingly it doesn’t. It means a scoring system did or didn’t clear a threshold, and thresholds can be gamed a little without lying about anything.
I also stopped taking the fast ones personally, which took longer than I expected given how many years I spent thinking rejection was supposed to mean something specific about me. Most of the time now it just means a form didn’t parse my resume the way its rubric wanted. That’s nothing, because it still costs me the job, but it’s a different kind of nothing than “you’re not good enough,” and my brain needed the spreadsheet to actually believe that distinction instead of just repeating it to myself.
I’m job hunting while also starting a graduate program this fall, which means the applications compete for time with everything else going on, and the spreadsheet habit is honestly the only thing that’s kept me from re-litigating every rejection in my head at 11 pm. Numbers instead of spirals. Not a cure, just a redirect.
The part I still haven’t figured out
Here’s what I don’t have an answer for. If a meaningful chunk of my rejections are coming from a system that scores keyword match rather than actual fit, and I get better at feeding that system the words it wants, am I actually getting better at showing my real experience, or just better at a different kind of test that has nothing to do with the job itself?
I genuinely don’t know. Some days it feels like a reasonable adaptation, the same as learning to write a cover letter that doesn’t sound like a form letter. Other days it feels like I’m training myself to perform for a machine instead of talking to the person who’ll actually decide whether to hire me, and that the two skills might be quietly pulling in different directions. I haven’t sorted out which one is true, or whether it’s both, and I’m not sure logging more timestamps is going to answer that particular question for me.
